message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the most important rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and federal law. For specific legal advice, consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization. | Category | Key Rights | Practical Tips | |----------|------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge a **maximum of one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Inspect the unit with the landlord before moving out and document any damage. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• Repairs must be made within a **reasonable time** after notice. | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep copies.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent or pay for repairs and deduct from rent (see “Rent‑Withholding” below). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease; late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are **reasonable** (not punitive). | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Rent‑Withholding** | • If the landlord fails to maintain habitability, you may **withhold rent** up to the amount needed for the repair, but you must:
1. Provide written notice to the landlord.
2. Pay the repair cost and keep receipts.
3. Return the withheld rent to the landlord after the repair is completed. | • Do not withhold rent without following the proper procedure; otherwise, you risk eviction. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must give **written notice**: 3 days for nonpayment, 30 days for lease termination (or 60 days if the lease is for 12 months or more).
• Eviction must be pursued through the court; a landlord cannot forcibly remove you. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you believe the notice is improper, consult an attorney or tenant‑rights group. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes (under the Fair Housing Act). | • Report any discriminatory practices to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or your local fair‑housing agency. | | **Lease Terms** | • The lease must be in writing if it lasts longer than one year.
• The lease cannot contain illegal or unconscionable provisions. | • Read the lease carefully before signing. | | **Right to Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, provided you follow the procedure above. | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Right to a Written Lease** | • Even if you sign a verbal lease, you have the right to a written copy. | • Request a written lease if you haven’t received one. | | **Right to a Safe Environment** | • Landlord must address pest infestations, mold, lead paint hazards, and other health risks. | • Report hazards immediately; if ignored, you may seek a court order. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Document any disturbances and notify the landlord. | | **Right to Sublet** | • The lease may prohibit subletting, but if it does, the landlord cannot unreasonably deny a sublet request. | • Ask for written permission if you plan to sublet. | | **Right to a Fair Rent Increase** | • Rent increases must be in accordance with the lease or, if the lease is silent, must comply with any local rent‑control ordinances (rare in Texas). | • Verify any increase is written and justified. | | **Right to a Refund of Unused Security Deposit** | • If you leave the unit in good condition, the landlord must refund the full deposit (minus any lawful deductions). | • Inspect the unit before moving out; take photos. | --- #### Quick Reference Checklist 1. **Get a written lease** – read it thoroughly. 2. **Document everything** – photos, videos, written notices, receipts. 3. **Know the notice periods** – 3 days for nonpayment, 30/60 days for lease termination. 4. **Report maintenance issues in writing** – keep copies. 5. **Understand your security deposit limits** – 1–2 months’ rent. 6. **Know your right to withhold rent** – follow the proper procedure. 7. **Know your right to privacy** – 24‑hour notice for entry. 8. **Know your right to a safe, habitable home** – landlord must fix major problems. 9. **Know your right to fair treatment** – no discrimination. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Tenant‑rights guides, complaint filing. | | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Fair housing information, landlord‑tenant resources. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Free legal clinics, mediation services. | | **HUD (U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development)** | Fair housing complaints, national resources. | | **Legal Aid of North Texas / Texas Legal Services** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance. | --- #### When to Seek Legal Help - **Unlawful eviction notice** or eviction proceeding. - **Discrimination claim** (e.g., denied entry or lease). - **Security deposit disputes** after moving out. - **Major habitability issues** that the landlord refuses to fix. - **Complex lease disputes** (e.g., subletting, rent increases). --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have strong protections against unfair treatment, unlawful eviction, and unsafe living conditions. Keep detailed records, communicate in writing, and know the statutory limits on deposits and rent. If you encounter a problem, use the resources above or consult an attorney.
